headline_marked: New documentary "NAZA" on Gaza killings receives [[25-minute standing ovation]] at Venice Film Festival
headline: New documentary "NAZA" on Gaza killings receives 25-minute standing ovation at Venice Film Festival
summary: An Oscar-winning Israeli filmmaking duo's documentary exploring alleged Israeli military actions in Gaza received a record-breaking standing ovation at the Venice Film Festival. The film features testimonies from 24 Israeli military insiders.
details: A new documentary titled "NAZA," directed by Oscar-winning Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, has premiered at the Venice Film Festival, focusing on the alleged mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza. The film received an extraordinary 25-minute standing ovation, reportedly setting a new record at the festival.

The documentary "NAZA" is described as a docu-drama that tells the story of the killing of a five-year-old Palestinian girl by Israeli forces. It includes testimonies from 24 Israeli military insiders, including intelligence officers and soldiers, who detail their experiences and alleged systematic killing of civilians.

The film was secretly shot over three years on rooftops across Tel Aviv, with the identities of interviewees concealed through digital alterations to their voices and appearances. The filmmakers' principal question to the Israeli officers and soldiers was to describe in detail "how it worked."

The title "NAZA" refers to an Israeli military acronym used as shorthand for civilian casualties, encompassing men, women, and children. The film builds upon investigations published between 2023 and 2025 by Israeli-Palestinian magazine 972 Magazine, Local Call, and The Guardian.

The strong reception at the Venice Film Festival has positioned "NAZA" as a potential frontrunner for the festival's top prize. Last year, a similar documentary, "The Voice of Hind Rajab," also received an enthusiastic response and a lengthy standing ovation, though it ultimately won the festival's second prize.

headline: Technical fault: Adani Godda unit shut down, adding pressure to BD grid
summary: An 800MW unit of the 1,600MW Godda plant in India has gone offline due to a boiler problem, intensifying load shedding in Bangladesh.
details: One of the two units of Adani Power’s 1,600MW Godda plant in Jharkhand, India, has shut down following a technical fault. The 800MW unit went offline around Thursday midnight after developing a boiler problem.
The shutdown occurred just as the plant had begun ramping up generation after weeks of reduced output caused by coal transportation disruptions.
Generation from Godda crossed 1,400MW on Thursday night before the unit tripped. Following the shutdown, supply fell to below 750MW
Bangladesh Power Development Board (PDB) officials confirmed that repair work will take at least 48 hours to begin, with full restoration requiring several more days.
The outage comes amid severe constraints due to shortages of gas, coal, and liquid fuel. Load shedding exceeded 2,500MW during the evening peak yesterday and may rise further.
The Godda plant had been operating at reduced capacity since mid-August due to railway congestion and excessive rainfall affecting coal supplies.
Overall generation has remained at 13,000-14,000MW against a demand of more than 16,000MW, leaving a substantial shortfall in the power supply.
caption:
A major power unit in India has tripped, further straining Bangladesh's electricity grid.

One of the two units of Adani Power’s 1,600MW Godda plant in Jharkhand, India, has shut down following a technical fault. The 800MW unit went offline around Thursday midnight after developing a boiler problem.

The shutdown occurred just as the plant had begun ramping up generation after weeks of reduced output caused by coal transportation disruptions.

Generation from Godda crossed 1,400MW on Thursday night before the unit tripped. Following the shutdown, supply fell to below 750MW

Bangladesh Power Development Board (PDB) officials confirmed that repair work will take at least 48 hours to begin, with full restoration requiring several more days.

The outage comes amid severe constraints due to shortages of gas, coal, and liquid fuel. Load shedding exceeded 2,500MW during the evening peak yesterday and may rise further.

The Godda plant had been operating at reduced capacity since mid-August due to railway congestion and excessive rainfall affecting coal supplies.

Overall generation has remained at 13,000-14,000MW against a demand of more than 16,000MW, leaving a substantial shortfall in the power supply.
